records.place: Cutchogue, North Fork of Long Island, New York

wine.name: Musée
wine.grapes: Bordeaux grapes in a blend that changes yearly: Merlot leads most vintages, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Petit Verdot; some years bring Cabernet Franc, Malbec or a little Syrah.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards at Cutchogue on the North Fork, on sandy glacial soils that drain fast, between Long Island Sound and the Peconic Bay.
wine.making: Made from the house's grapes of the North Fork. By the house's own account every wine of the cellar is fermented with the wild yeasts of the place rather than bought cultures. The wine is then aged in barrel before bottling, and its blend is chosen again with each vintage.
wine.glass: Black cherry, black plum and cedar with dried violet, lead pencil and liquorice, and dried mushroom as it ages; medium in body, with crisp acidity and chewy, firm tannin that softens over the years.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release, it gains savoury depth over its first decade and a strong vintage keeps well beyond it.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: French for museum: the house's leading red blend, under a label made from an artist's work.
The American Viticultural Area of the northern fork, approved in 1986.

records.table: Chuck Close made the first label of Musée, the 2005, and the wine behind it heads the range of Bedell Cellars at Cutchogue on the North Fork: a blend of the Bordeaux grapes, led by Merlot in most years, firm and savoury enough to want a decanter.
records.story: Bedell Cellars began in 1980, when its founder planted his first vines on a farm at Cutchogue, seven years after the first vinifera went into a potato field in the same village. Through the 1980s and 1990s the house built its name on Merlot, the grape that leads on the North Fork, and in 1986 the North Fork of Long Island won its own American Viticultural Area. At the turn of the century, in 1999 by the house's account and in 2000 by the press, the estate was sold to a group led by Michael Lynne (1941 to 2019), the film executive of New Line Cinema, who kept the founder on as winemaker and set out to raise the house to the serious end of the fork. He brought in contemporary artists to make the labels, and his friend the painter and photographer Chuck Close (1940 to 2021) made the label of the first Musée, the 2005. In 2013 the house's Merlot of 2009 was poured at the luncheon of the presidential inauguration in Washington, by the house's account the first New York wine served at an inauguration. The house holds that it ferments every wine with wild yeasts alone. Whether Long Island makes a red to keep is the question Musée answers for the North Fork.

others.name: Merlot
others.note: The house's grape of record; the 2009 was poured at the inaugural luncheon of 2013.

others.name: Taste Red
others.note: A second red blend of the house, for drinking sooner than Musée.

traps: Musée is a blend whose grapes change with the vintage, not a varietal Merlot, though Merlot is the grape the house is known for.
The wine poured at the 2013 inauguration was the 2009 Merlot, not Musée.
Bedell is at Cutchogue on the North Fork, not in the Hamptons on the South Fork.

records.place: Peconic, North Fork of Long Island, New York

wine.name: Old Vines Merlot
wine.grapes: Merlot, from the house's oldest vines.
wine.sites: The oldest blocks of the house's estate vineyard at Peconic on the North Fork, planted in its first decades on sandy, fast draining glacial soils.
wine.making: Made only in vintages the house judges able to give a wine of depth and long life, from its oldest Merlot vines. The wine is aged in barrel and then held back in the cellar for years, so it reaches the market long after the vintage, and the house keeps a library of older bottles and magnums.
wine.glass: Black plum, dark cherry and raspberry with cedar, cigar box and leather, mocha and black tea as it ages; medium in body, with fresh acidity, smooth, fine tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Released with age already on it, it keeps improving in a cool cellar; by the house's own tastings of its library its Old Vines reds peak at fifteen to twenty years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; stand an older bottle upright and decant it gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The house's tier from its oldest vineyard blocks, made only in strong vintages.
The American Viticultural Area of the northern fork, approved in 1986.

records.table: Years in the cellar before release set the Old Vines Merlot of Lenz Winery apart: from the oldest vines of an early North Fork estate, planted at Peconic from 1978, it arrives savoury and ready. Decant an older bottle off its sediment.
records.story: The Lenz Winery began in 1978, when the Lenz family planted vines on a farm at Peconic on the North Fork, close to Cutchogue, where Long Island's vinifera had gone into the ground five years before. Theirs was one of the island's early estates. In 1988, ten years on, the winery passed to new owners, who kept the founders' name on the label and set the house on its course of patient, long lived wines. After 1993, a strong year for reds, the house began to hold back part of its Old Vines Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, which became the library from which it sells older bottles and magnums. It also took to comparative blind tastings, setting its wines beside well known wines of Europe and California to test the North Fork's claim. The Old Vines tier sits at the top of the range, drawn from the oldest blocks and made only when the house thinks a year can give depth and long life. What time does to a North Fork Merlot is what the Old Vines shows, and few houses on the island let a guest taste it.

others.name: Old Vines Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: The red of the same Old Vines tier, from the house's old Cabernet Sauvignon vines.

others.name: Estate Selection Merlot
others.note: The house's estate Merlot below the Old Vines tier; the house's own notes call the Old Vines the same, only more so.

traps: Lenz releases its Old Vines Merlot years after the vintage, so an old date on a new bottle is the house style, not old stock.
Lenz is at Peconic on the North Fork, not on the South Fork among the Hamptons estates.

records.place: Aquebogue, North Fork of Long Island, New York

wine.name: Chenin Blanc
wine.sites: The family's estate at Aquebogue on the North Fork, a former potato farm, with the Chenin Blanc first found in an abandoned vineyard bought in 1989 and planted further in 2000 and 2005.
wine.making: Fermented slowly at cool temperatures in stainless steel tanks, with no oak, to keep its fruit and its acidity. It is bottled young under screw cap, which the house was the first on Long Island to take up, by the local press, to hold its freshness.
wine.glass: Grapefruit, green apple and pineapple over pear and a touch of guava; dry, crisp and racy, light to medium in body, with a savoury, briny edge from the sea air.
wine.ageing: Made to drink in its first few years for its freshness, though a good vintage keeps and grows rounder over five years or so.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass. Oysters and white fish suit it.

label.means: The grape of the Loire's Vouvray and Savennières, rare on Long Island.
The American Viticultural Area of the northern fork, approved in 1986.

records.table: An abandoned vineyard bought in 1989 gave Paumanok Vineyards the vines of its Chenin Blanc, the white of record at its family estate at Aquebogue: fermented cool in steel, unoaked and under screw cap, dry and racy with grapefruit and a briny edge. Pour it cold with oysters.
records.story: Paumanok Vineyards was founded in 1983 on a former potato farm at Aquebogue on the North Fork, when a couple planted its first vines: she came from Germany, from a family of vintners, and he was born in Lebanon. The Chenin Blanc came by accident. In 1989 the family bought an abandoned vineyard planted to many grapes, Chenin Blanc among them, and meant to pull most of them out; the story goes that the Chenin was spared, a little wine was made from it, and they liked it. They kept it, planted more in 2000 and 2005 and a new clone in 2012, and Chenin Blanc became the house's white of record, by the house's own account the first made in New York. By the local press it became, in 2007, the first winery on Long Island to use screw caps. In 2018 the family bought Palmer Vineyards nearby, also founded in 1983, and from then the founders' son made the wine of both. Paumanok's Chenin carries the North Fork's acid and salt in a grape few guests expect to meet there.

others.name: Riesling
others.note: A white from the estate's own Riesling vines at Aquebogue, one of the grapes it grows.

records.place: Sagaponack, The Hamptons, Long Island, New York

wine.name: Estate Rosé
wine.grapes: Merlot, the larger part, with Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay and small touches of other grapes, white and red, in a blend that changes each year.
wine.sites: The estate's vineyard at Sagaponack on the South Fork, once potato fields near the Atlantic shore, on the South Fork's loam.
wine.making: Each grape is picked in its own wave, at the moment the house judges it ready, to keep the character of each. The wines are made separately and blended, and the rosé is given extended contact with its lees before it is bottled young for the summer.
wine.glass: Pale salmon pink; honeysuckle and violet on the nose with ripe, fresh berry fruit and a delicate creamy, yeasty note from its lees; dry, light in body and crisp.
wine.ageing: Made to drink in the summer after the vintage, it keeps its freshness for a year or two.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: The house's estate rosé, first released under that name in 1996, distinct from its Summer in a Bottle range.
The American Viticultural Area of the whole island, approved in 2001.

records.table: Sagaponack on the South Fork gives Wölffer Estate its Estate Rosé, a pale, dry and crisp blend led by Merlot with several grapes, white and red, which grew up with the Hamptons' taste for rosé; serve it cold.
records.story: In 1978 a Hamburg born investor bought a parcel of farmland with a farmhouse among the potato fields of Sagaponack on the South Fork, and in 1988 he planted his first vineyard there, of Chardonnay, under the name Sagpond Vineyards. A German winemaker joined in 1992, and by the house's timeline the first Sagpond rosé followed in 1993. The winery took the founder's name, Wölffer, in 1996 by its own timeline, and the first Estate Rosé was released that year. The pale, dry Estate Rosé grew with the Hamptons' taste for rosé, and the estate kept horses and stables beside its vines. The founder died in a swimming accident in Brazil on the last day of 2008, and his children carried the estate on with the winemaker. The house later added the Summer in a Bottle rosés, a separate line, and a cuvée of Merlot from its oldest field, planted in 1990, named for the founder. The Estate Rosé is the East Coast's lesson in pale, dry rosé, grown on an American island.

wine.name: Bergen Road
wine.grapes: A blend of the Bordeaux grapes led by Merlot, with Cabernet Sauvignon and, by the year, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot or Malbec.
wine.sites: The family's waterfront farm at Mattituck on the bluffs above Long Island Sound, on sandy glacial soils, farmed with biodynamic principles from its first plantings.
wine.making: Made only in the vintages the family judges strong enough, from the estate's own grapes, the share of each Bordeaux grape decided vintage by vintage. It is aged in oak barrels for well over a year before bottling.
wine.glass: Damson plum, raspberry and blackberry with cedar and a hint of green pepper; medium in body, with lively acidity and fine grained tannin coated in fruit.
wine.ageing: Firm when young, it opens after five years or so and a strong vintage keeps well into its second decade.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The house's flagship red blend, made only in strong vintages.
The American Viticultural Area of the northern fork, approved in 1986.

records.table: Biodynamic farming above Long Island Sound at Mattituck shapes Bergen Road, Macari Vineyards' flagship red: a Merlot led blend of the Bordeaux grapes, made only in strong years. Firm and fresh, it opens with an hour or two in a decanter.
records.story: The Macari family owned a waterfront farm at Mattituck, on the bluffs above Long Island Sound, for decades before it held a vine; by the house's account the family had owned the land for about half a century. In 1995 father, son and daughter in law planted the first vineyard there and founded Macari Vineyards, on an island whose vinifera went back only to 1973, at Cutchogue. From the first plantings the family farmed by biodynamic principles, making its own compost and keeping a herd of cattle, longhorns at first, for their manure and for the horn preparations biodynamic farming uses. Bergen Road became the house's flagship red, a blend of the Bordeaux grapes made only when the family judges a vintage strong enough, its blend set afresh each time. Bergen Road brings biodynamic farming on Long Island to the glass, and shows how the North Fork's Merlot and Cabernet are blended.

cards.back: 1995, on a waterfront farm above Long Island Sound that the family had owned for about half a century.

questions.q: A guest asks what Macari Vineyards' Bergen Road is. Which answer fits?
opts: A Merlot led blend of the Bordeaux grapes
A varietal Cabernet Franc from the bluffs
A sparkling wine made by the traditional method
A Syrah from the warmest block
questions.exp: Bergen Road blends Merlot with Cabernet Sauvignon and, by the year, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot or Malbec; the house's Cabernet Franc is a separate varietal wine.

questions.q: Macari Vineyards farms its Mattituck estate by biodynamic principles. When did that begin?
opts: With the first plantings of 1995
In 1973, with Long Island's first vinifera
After a sale of the estate in 2010
In 1986, with the North Fork appellation
questions.exp: The family followed biodynamic principles from the first plantings of 1995; 1973 is the year of the first vinifera at Cutchogue, before the estate existed.

report: The pick stands: the house's own page calls Bergen Road its flagship red blend, made only in premium vintages, and Decanter says the same; Alexandra goes in others as the reserve red, its exact place in the range not confirmed beyond one listing.
Founded 1995 rests on the house and two guides; the family members are living and are not named, and the wine Alexandra is named for a living member of the family, which the record does not say.

Biodynamic principles from the first plantings, the home made compost and the longhorn cattle rest on the house's account through two press summaries; the house's own search did not return the word biodynamic, so the checker may want the house's page.
The land in the family since the 1960s rests on one press account and the house's over half a century; it is hedged as the house's account.

The blend varies: Merlot led in 2010, 2015, 2020 and 2021 by Jancis Robinson, the house, Decanter and Forbes; French oak up to twenty two months is Forbes for 2021 only, so the record says oak barrels for well over a year.
The origin of the name Bergen Road (the estate's address is on Bergen Avenue) was not sourced and is not taught.
The Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet Franc in others rest on the region record and the plan only; the glass note is not drawn from an independent tasting note.

changed: story and card: was the land in the family since the 1960s; now about half a century before the vines, since the house and Wine Folly say over fifty years and the 1960s rests on one account.
story and card: was a herd of longhorn cattle; now a herd of cattle, longhorns at first, since a family interview says the herd is now mixed.
story and trap: the second tasting room at Cutchogue is cut, since the house's own page says that site was relaunched under another name in 2022: a fact true only for some years.
wine.glass: was an untested note with graphite; now damson plum, raspberry, blackberry, cedar and a hint of green pepper, medium bodied with fine grained tannin, by the Wine Folly guide and VinePair.
sources: Dan's Papers gives way to the Wine Folly guide's wine notes.
open: The origin of the name Bergen Road is not taught; the estate's address is Bergen Avenue.
